title: How to Deal With Iran
gist: Marko Jukic argues the U.S.-Iran war stalemate is driven not by the Strait of Hormuz but by Iran's commoditized, strike-resistant drone and missile industrial base, which has burned 62 percent of U.S. Patriot and THAAD interceptor stocks in five months and cannot be bombed away. Because closure of the uniquely non-circumventable strait threatens a global depression, he says the only near-term exit is 'economic relief for bombing restraint' - Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, a Montreux-style Iran-Oman transit-fee regime, and sanctions relief - while the U.S. spends five to ten years reindustrializing, electrifying, and drilling to erode Iran's edge.

insights.claim: The 14-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding signed by Trump and Iran on 17 June, which set a 60-day ceasefire and unhindered Hormuz transit, collapsed within days when Iran resumed striking civilian ships in the strait.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Signed frameworks with Iran have already failed once; price ceasefire headlines as reversible, not as durable de-risking of tanker and energy exposure.
insights.quote: Iran began striking civilian ships in the strait just days later.

insights.claim: Oil and natural gas supply 58 percent of all global energy consumption, and the Persian Gulf region produces 31 percent of world crude and 18 percent of world natural gas while accounting for 42 percent of global oil exports and 27 percent of global LNG exports.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: These are the base rates for sizing any Hormuz disruption scenario; the export shares (42%/27%) matter more than production shares for marginal price setting.

insights.claim: Roughly 20 percent of the world's daily oil and gas supply transited the Strait of Hormuz before the war, and continued closure risks a prolonged global economic depression rather than a transient price spike.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: The author frames sustained closure as a depression-scale event, implying convex upside in energy and downside in equities the longer closure persists.

insights.claim: A Hormuz-driven depression would define the Trump administration's legacy negatively via plummeting stock markets, skyrocketing prices, rising unemployment, and unpredictable shortages, all but guaranteeing a Democratic victory in the 2028 U.S. presidential election.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Frames a domestic political incentive for Washington to concede to Iran quickly - a bias toward a deal rather than escalation.
insights.locator: A global economic depression of this scale

insights.claim: A war-induced economic disaster would discredit not just Trump personally but the entire international populist current, because populist leaders who accidentally damage constituents' interests forfeit their claim against establishment leaders who damage them intentionally.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Implies multi-year political regime shift risk in developed markets - a swing toward redistributionist policy that reprices tax, labor, and defense budgets.
insights.quote: Populist politics are a lost cause if populist leaders accidentally cause as much damage to their constituents’ interests as establishment leaders cause intentionally.

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz is a red herring: the core driver of the conflict is Iran's efficient, robust, technologically advanced military-industrial base, which has let Iran bomb the region at will for the five months since fighting began on 28 February.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Reframes the tradeable variable from shipping-lane diplomacy to Iranian production capacity - meaning ceasefires that ignore industry are unstable.
insights.locator: The Strait of Hormuz is nonetheless something of a red herring

insights.claim: Long-range precision-guided munitions capable of evading air defenses, once the technological foundation of U.S. global military supremacy, have been commoditized by the same globalization and industrial-diffusion processes that deindustrialized the developed world and grew the developing world, especially China.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Structural erosion of the U.S. defense moat: legacy platform primes lose relevance against volume producers of cheap munitions.
insights.quote: this technological marvel has been commoditized
insights.locator: Unfortunately, this technological marvel

insights.claim: Iran deserves credit for inventing and popularizing the low-cost fixed-wing one-way attack drone via the Shahed-131 and Shahed-136, designs since imitated by the Russian, Chinese, and even U.S. militaries - a rare case of a heavily sanctioned developing country originating a technology validated by all military superpowers.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'sanctions will exhaust Iran's arsenal' thesis; treat Iranian drone output as an indigenous, replenishable industrial capability.
insights.locator: Iran has not improperly acquired advanced technology

insights.claim: Iran launched an Iranian-made satellite on an Iranian-made rocket in 2009 - before Italy or South Korea achieved the milestone - and since 2020 has added its own military reconnaissance satellites to orbit, supplementing Russian and Chinese satellite intelligence used for targeting.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Iranian targeting is not fully dependent on Chinese or Russian ISR, so cutting off allied intelligence would not blind Iranian strikes.
insights.locator: By the same token, many people would likely be surprised

insights.claim: No reliable countermeasures to Iran's drones and missiles yet exist, and none are likely without several more years of experimentation, manufacturing expansion, and major cost reductions - the technology is simply too new for countermeasures to have developed and diffused.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Sets a multi-year clock on counter-drone capability, favoring firms that can scale cheap interceptors over incumbents selling exquisite systems.
insights.locator: As of yet, no reliable countermeasures

insights.claim: The stalemate exists because the developed world's technological stagnation, deindustrialization, and institutional sclerosis let Iran rather than Ohio become the first to mass-produce the weapons of the future.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Positions U.S. industrial capacity - not diplomacy - as the binding constraint, supporting a structural reindustrialization and defense-manufacturing theme.
insights.quote: the developed world’s technological stagnation, deindustrialization, and institutional sclerosis have allowed Iran rather than Ohio to jump ahead and be the first to mass-produce the weapons of the future.

insights.claim: Proposals to circumvent the Iranian threat with new pipelines or alternative maritime routes are farcical because Iranian drones and missiles can strike land or sea targets for thousands of kilometers in any direction, and launchers can be moved and fired from deep inland.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Discount 'bypass pipeline' narratives as a resolution catalyst for Gulf energy risk premia.
insights.quote: You cannot move the entire oil-producing Persian Gulf region outside the range of Iranian bombs.
insights.locator: This is of course why proposals to “circumvent”

insights.claim: Iran's drone and missile production cannot be decapitated like a nuclear program because it depends on ordinary industrial capacity, not two or three top-secret sites: Shahed-style engines are nicknamed 'flying lawnmowers' and are identical in design and near in horsepower to lawnmower engines.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Cheap-commodity supply chains are strike-resistant; counterproliferation logic that works on nukes does not transfer to drones.
insights.locator: Proposals to simply “take out” Iran’s drone

insights.claim: Iran is a relatively industrialized country of 93 million people, the size of Alaska and just as mountainous, so eliminating its ability to manufacture something as basic as lawnmowers would require a years-long bombing campaign on the scale of the Allied bombing of Nazi Germany - and Iran has already buried key production and storage underground.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Any 'short sharp air campaign ends this' scenario is mispriced; the base case is prolonged disruption or a negotiated settlement.
insights.locator: Iran is a relatively industrialized country of 93 million

insights.claim: Removing the Iranian regime by force would require a ground invasion of millions of troops over years with no guarantee of success, hundreds of thousands of U.S. casualties, and a possibly multi-decade depression as Iran retaliated indiscriminately against all Gulf energy infrastructure and Israeli civilian targets.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Assigns near-zero probability to a regime-change resolution path; the tail risk is escalation, not clean victory.

insights.so_what: Decapitation strikes hardened rather than destabilized Iranian policy - expect successor negotiators to be less, not more, flexible.

insights.claim: There is no tight relationship between impoverishment and regime change: Bashar al-Assad's far more brittle and less well-resourced Syrian regime took nearly fourteen years to collapse under economic desolation, so betting on Iranian collapse under blockade is a losing game of economic chicken.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Maximum-pressure sanctions are unlikely to resolve the supply shock within an investable horizon; assume persistence.

themes.theme: Deal Architecture: Economic Relief for Bombing Restraint

insights.claim: Just as 'sanctions relief for nuclear restraint' was the unavoidable dynamic in nuclear talks, 'economic relief for bombing restraint' will be the unavoidable dynamic in any Hormuz negotiation, with U.S. carrots including oil-export sanctions relief, unfreezing Iranian funds held abroad, and coordinating direct investment or reconstruction funds.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: A deal path implies Iranian barrels returning to market - a bearish medium-term crude catalyst that partly offsets the bullish closure premium.
insights.quote: “economic relief for bombing restraint” is going to remain the unavoidable dynamic

insights.claim: The realistic settlement is mutual face-saving: Israel withdraws from occupied areas of Lebanon leaving the Lebanese military in control with UN-coordinated third-country assistance, while Iran orders Hezbollah to stay proactively but tacitly disarmed there, with the U.S. as guarantor and intermediary since Israel and Iran will not talk directly.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Concrete deal template to monitor - a UN-coordinated force deploying to southern Lebanon would be the leading indicator that Hormuz reopens.

insights.claim: Iran expects $20-40 billion in annual transit fees from the strait, roughly a tenth of its GDP, arriving straight into government coffers with little additional effort.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Quantifies Iran's reservation price for a deal; any settlement not delivering on this order of magnitude is unlikely to stick.

insights.claim: Latest reported proposals have Iran and Oman managing the strait bilaterally - Iran handling inbound traffic, Oman outbound - with free passage initially, then safe-navigation fees and possibly much higher fees on U.S. or Israeli-linked ships as war reparations, and the Trump administration is reportedly inclined to accept.

insights.claim: The legal objection to Iranian control of the strait is weaker than it looks because neither the United States nor Iran - nor the UAE nor Israel - are parties to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Removes a perceived legal blocker to a deal, raising the odds of a negotiated Hormuz regime that markets may be underpricing.

insights.claim: The 1936 Montreux Convention governing Turkey's control of the Bosphorus and Dardanelles - allowing minimal passage fees and closure when Turkey feels threatened - is the precedent for formally recognizing Iran's at least partial influence over the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: A named legal template negotiators can copy; its appearance in official language would signal a deal is close.

insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: A formalized Iranian closure right would embed a permanent, recurring geopolitical option premium in Gulf energy and tanker insurance.

insights.claim: Excepting Hormuz from freedom of navigation will not cascade to global shipping because it is a wholly unique chokepoint: no comparable passage has the entire planet depending on the commodities continuously exiting it, and it is the only major chokepoint a ship cannot physically circumvent.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Kills the 'precedent risk' argument against a deal and explains why Hormuz risk premia should not be extrapolated to Malacca or Suez.

insights.claim: Chokepoint leverage has collapsed everywhere except Hormuz: the Houthis' 2023-2025 closure of Bab-el-Mandeb was invisible without reading the news, and Egypt's 1967-1975 closure of the Suez Canal is forgotten because ships simply rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Historical base rate for pricing chokepoint disruptions: reroutable straits produce freight-rate noise, not macro shocks.
insights.quote: Egypt closed the Suez Canal from 1967 to 1975, with the outcome that nobody today even remembers it happened because cargo ships just began going around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa instead.

insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Deflates copycat-toll fears in Southeast Asia; the marginal cost of rerouting caps any imitator's pricing power.

themes.theme: Interceptor Depletion and Defense Industrial Reform

insights.claim: After five months of war the U.S. pre-war stockpile of 2,200 Patriot missiles and 452 THAAD missiles has been depleted to 827 and 278 respectively - a 62 percent drawdown the author calls a completely unsustainable rate.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Hard interceptor inventory numbers imply a forced multi-year replenishment cycle and a hard ceiling on how long the U.S. can sustain its current posture.
insights.quote: depleting your missile defenses by 62% in a few months is a completely unsustainable rate
insights.locator: the pre-war stockpile of 2200 Patriot missiles

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia has reportedly depleted 86 percent of its stockpiled Patriot PAC-3 interceptors since February, faring worse than the U.S. itself.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Gulf air-defense exhaustion is a near-term escalation risk and a large latent order book for interceptor manufacturers.
insights.locator: Gulf allies have fared even worse

insights.claim: Incumbent defense contractors are unlikely to replenish stockpiles fast enough or develop cheaper interceptors, so the Pentagon should force internal efficiency and volume-production reforms while introducing competition from defense startups like Anduril and Ukrainian defense companies closer to the practical cutting edge of modern warfare.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: An explicit share-shift call from legacy primes toward new-entrant and Ukrainian producers of low-cost munitions.
insights.locator: Incumbent defense contractors are unlikely to replenish

insights.claim: The U.S. military has already procured thousands of Merops drones from Ukraine to destroy Shahed-style drones in flight, and the author argues the goal should be a stockpile of millions of such interceptor drones to neutralize the Iranian drone threat across the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Signals the winning counter-drone architecture is cheap attritable interceptors at million-unit scale, not exquisite missiles - a procurement regime change.
insights.locator: The U.S. military has already procured thousands of Merops

insights.claim: Iran has adapted to the new meta of mass drone warfare by burying key facilities underground while U.S. and allied military and industrial facilities remain above ground, compounding the cost asymmetry in which cheap Iranian weapons get past expensive Western ones.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Hardening and dispersal of Western basing and industrial sites is an underappreciated multi-year capex theme.
insights.quote: Iran’s weapons are just better than ours.

insights.claim: China is not particularly interested in assisting Iran's interventionist foreign policy and so would not be expected to shift its tremendous industrial weight in Iran's favor.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Caps the escalation ceiling: a Chinese-backed Iranian arsenal surge is not the base case, limiting the tail risk in Gulf energy.

insights.claim: Iran's leverage can be neutralized by cutting global dependence on Persian Gulf oil and gas two ways at once: drilling for more oil and gas everywhere else in the world, and replacing fossil-fuel-powered technology with electrically powered technology.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: A both/and energy frame implies simultaneous structural support for non-Gulf upstream and for electrification supply chains.

insights.claim: The dichotomy between drilling and gas-guzzling cars versus a green low-energy economy must be discarded in favor of energy abundance and independence, meaning drilling, fracking, and coal mining are cheerfully pursued alongside nuclear power plants, solar photovoltaic farms, and fleets of self-driving electric taxis.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: An abundance-coalition policy frame that would be bullish for hydrocarbon producers and nuclear/solar/AV buildout simultaneously.
insights.quote: The goal must be energy abundance and independence

insights.claim: Defense reform, reindustrialization, electrification, and resource extraction will not produce a favorable peace in the short term but, intelligently and vigorously pursued, could erode Iran's military-technological edge and shift the balance of power decisively in as little as five or ten years.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: Sets an explicit 5-10 year horizon for the counter-Iran industrial theme - a duration over which to underwrite defense-industrial and energy capex exposure.
insights.locator: Defense reform, reindustrialization, electrification

insights.claim: A failed game of economic chicken with Iran could lock the Western world into a generation of economically redistributionist politics indifferent to the fates of U.S. allies in the Middle East and uninterested in improving developed-world military or industrial capacity.
insights.speaker: Marko Jukic
insights.so_what: The long-horizon risk is a policy regime that abandons defense and industrial investment - a structural headwind for the entire reindustrialization trade.
